question: What are the main provisions of the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' signed in July 2025?
text:
President Donald Trump signed the **One Big Beautiful Bill Act** (H.R. 1, **Public Law 119-21**) on **July 4, 2025**. The law made many of the 2017 tax cuts permanent, reduced projected federal spending on Medicaid and food assistance, and increased funding for immigration enforcement and defense. ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ21/html/PLAW-119publ21.htm))

| Area | Main provisions |
|---|---|
| **Individual taxes** | Made the 2017 individual income-tax rates and larger standard deduction permanent. Raised the maximum child tax credit to **$2,200 per qualifying child** for 2025 and temporarily raised the state and local tax (SALT) deduction cap to **$40,000** for most filers in 2025, with a return to **$10,000** in 2030. Created temporary deductions for qualifying tips, overtime premiums, certain auto-loan interest, and eligible seniors for **2025–2028**. ([everycrsreport.com](https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2025-07-29_R48611_bb2f5cc1bdc7bb3e919d12ec54e7dce391eb79af.html?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Business taxes and children’s accounts** | Restored immediate deductions for qualifying equipment and domestic research expenses. Created tax-advantaged **“Trump Accounts”** for children, with a **$1,000 federal contribution** for eligible U.S. citizen children born from 2025 through 2028. ([everycrsreport.com](https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2025-07-29_R48611_bb2f5cc1bdc7bb3e919d12ec54e7dce391eb79af.html?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Medicaid and health coverage** | Added work or other qualifying-activity requirements for many adults covered through Medicaid expansion, tightened eligibility checks, and limited some ways states finance Medicaid. It also tightened eligibility for certain Affordable Care Act marketplace subsidies and created a **$50 billion rural health program**. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/PDF/R48633/R48633.1.pdf)) |
| **Food assistance (SNAP)** | Expanded work requirements to more adults, narrowed noncitizen eligibility, and shifted some program costs to states, including a share of benefit costs for states with higher payment-error rates. ([everycrsreport.com](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/R48552.html?utm_source=openai)) |
| **Immigration and defense** | Funded border barriers, immigration enforcement, and expanded detention capacity, including **$45 billion for immigration detention**. The defense title provided about **$156 billion** for priorities including shipbuilding, missile defense, and munitions. ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ21/html/PLAW-119publ21.htm)) |
| **Energy and student loans** | Ended federal electric-vehicle tax credits early, accelerated the phaseout of several other clean-energy incentives, and expanded federal oil and gas leasing. It also capped federal borrowing for graduate students and parents, ended new Grad PLUS loans with transition exceptions, and restructured repayment options. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/faqs-for-modification-of-sections-25c-25d-25e-30c-30d-45l-45w-and-179d-under-public-law-119-21-139-stat-72-july-4-2025-commonly-known-as-the-one-big-beautiful-bill-obbb?ref=themanifestarchive.com&utm_source=openai)) |

The law also **raised the federal debt ceiling by $5 trillion**. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that, relative to its January 2025 baseline, the law would **increase federal deficits by $3.4 trillion over fiscal years 2025–2034**, before additional interest costs: projected revenue fell by more than projected spending did. ([govinfo.gov](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ21/html/PLAW-119publ21.htm))
